subject: Physics
text: The order of coloured rings in a carbon resistor is red, yellow, blue and silver. The resistance of the carbon resistor is: (a) 24×10^6 Ω ± 5% (b) 24×10^6 Ω ± 10% (c) 34×10^4 Ω ± 10% (d) 26×10^4 Ω ± 5%
modelAnswer: (b) 24×10^6 Ω ± 10%. Red = 2, Yellow = 4, Blue = multiplier 10^6, Silver = tolerance ±10%. So resistance = 24 × 10^6 Ω ± 10%.
keyPoints: Colour code: 1st band = 1st digit, 2nd band = 2nd digit, 3rd band = multiplier, 4th band = tolerance

subject: Physics
text: A circular coil carrying a current I has radius R and number of turns N. If all the three, i.e. the current I, radius R and number of turns N are doubled, then, magnetic field at its centre becomes: (a) Double (b) Half (c) Four times (d) One fourth
modelAnswer: (a) Double. B = μ0NI/2R. Doubling N, I and R gives B' = μ0(2N)(2I)/(2×2R) = 2×(μ0NI/2R) = 2B, i.e. B doubles.
keyPoints: B at centre of coil = μ0NI/(2R)
New N,I,R all ×2 → numerator ×4, denominator ×2 → net ×2

subject: Physics
text: An object is kept on the principal axis of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm, at a distance of 15 cm from its pole. The image formed by the mirror is: (a) Virtual and magnified (b) Virtual and diminished (c) Real and magnified (d) Real and diminished
modelAnswer: (c) Real and magnified. Using mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f with u = −15 cm, f = −10 cm: 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = −1/10 + 1/15 = −1/30, so v = −30 cm. Magnification m = −v/u = −(−30)/(−15) = −2, i.e. real, inverted and magnified (2×).

subject: Physics
text: Einstein's photoelectric equation is: (a) Emax = hλ − φ0 (b) Emax = hc/λ − φ0 (c) Emax = hν + φ0 (d) Emax = hc/λ + φ0
modelAnswer: (b) Emax = hc/λ − φ0. The maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectron equals the photon energy (hν = hc/λ) minus the work function φ0 of the metal.
keyPoints: Photoelectric equation: Emax = hν − φ0 = hc/λ − φ0
Energy of incident photon minus work function

subject: Physics
text: In Bohr's model of hydrogen atom, radius of the first orbit of an electron is r0. Then, radius of the third orbit is: (a) r0/9 (b) r0 (c) 3r0 (d) 9r0
modelAnswer: (d) 9r0. Radius of nth Bohr orbit rn = n²r0. For n = 3, r3 = 9r0.

subject: Physics
text: In a potentiometer experiment, balancing length is found to be 120 cm for a cell E1 of emf 2V. What will be the balancing length for another cell E2 of emf 1·5V? (No other changes are made in the experiment.)
modelAnswer: Balancing length is proportional to emf (l ∝ E) since the potential gradient is unchanged. l1/E1 = l2/E2 → l2 = E2×l1/E1 = 1·5×120/2 = 90 cm.
keyPoints: l ∝ emf for same potential gradient

subject: Physics
text: How will you convert a moving coil galvanometer into a voltmeter?
modelAnswer: Connect a high resistance (a suitable 'multiplier' resistance) in series with the galvanometer coil. The value of resistance R needed for a range of V volts is R = (V/Ig) − G, where Ig is the full-scale deflection current and G is the galvanometer resistance.
keyPoints: Series high resistance converts galvanometer to voltmeter

subject: Physics
text: A moving charged particle q travelling along the positive x-axis enters a uniform magnetic field B. When will the force acting on q be maximum?
modelAnswer: The magnetic force F = qvB sinθ is maximum when the velocity v is perpendicular to the magnetic field B (θ = 90°), giving Fmax = qvB.

subject: Physics
text: Why is the core of a transformer laminated?
modelAnswer: The core is laminated (made of thin, insulated sheets of soft iron) to reduce eddy currents induced in the core, thereby minimising energy losses (heating) due to eddy currents and improving efficiency.
keyPoints: Reduces energy loss as heat, improves efficiency

subject: Physics
text: Ordinary (i.e. unpolarised) light is incident on the surface of a transparent material at the polarising angle. If it is partly reflected and partly refracted, what is the angle between the reflected and the refracted rays?
modelAnswer: The angle between the reflected and refracted rays is 90° (this is Brewster's law condition, where the reflected ray is completely plane polarised).
keyPoints: At polarising angle, reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular

subject: Physics
text: Define coherent sources of light.
modelAnswer: Coherent sources are two (or more) sources of light that emit light waves of the same frequency (wavelength) and are either in phase or have a constant (time-independent) phase difference between them.

subject: Physics
text: Name a material which is used in making control rods in a nuclear reactor.
modelAnswer: Cadmium (or Boron) is used as the material for control rods in a nuclear reactor, since it strongly absorbs neutrons.
keyPoints: Control rod material: Cadmium or Boron
Absorbs neutrons to control chain reaction

subject: Physics
text: Define current density. Write an expression which connects current density with drift speed.
modelAnswer: Current density (J) is the amount of current flowing per unit cross-sectional area of a conductor, in the direction normal to the area: J = I/A (unit: A/m²). It is related to drift speed vd by J = nevd, where n is the free electron number density and e is the electronic charge.
keyPoints: n = free electron density, e = electronic charge, vd = drift speed

subject: Physics
text: A long horizontal wire P carries a current of 50A. It is rigidly fixed. Another wire Q is placed directly above and parallel to P. The weight per unit length of the wire Q is 0·025 Nm⁻¹ and it carries a current of 25A. Find the distance 'r' of the wire Q from the wire P so that the wire Q remains at rest.
modelAnswer: For Q to remain at rest, the magnetic force per unit length between the wires must balance the weight per unit length of Q. F/l = μ0I1I2/(2πr) = weight/length. So (4π×10⁻⁷×50×25)/(2πr) = 0·025 → (2×10⁻⁷×50×25)/r = 0·025 → 2·5×10⁻⁴/r = 0·025 → r = 2·5×10⁻⁴/0·025 = 0·01 m = 1 cm.

subject: Physics
text: (i) Explain Curie's law for a paramagnetic substance. (ii) A rectangular coil having 60 turns and area of 0·4m² is held at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 5×10⁻⁵T. Calculate the magnetic flux passing through it.
modelAnswer: (i) Curie's law states that the magnetic susceptibility (χ) of a paramagnetic substance is inversely proportional to its absolute temperature: χ = C/T, where C is the Curie constant. As temperature increases, thermal agitation disturbs the alignment of magnetic dipoles, reducing magnetisation. (ii) Flux Φ = NBA = 60 × 5×10⁻⁵ × 0·4 = 1·2×10⁻³ Wb.

subject: Physics
text: What is motional emf? State any two factors on which it depends.
modelAnswer: Motional emf is the emf induced in a conductor when it moves through a magnetic field such that it cuts magnetic field lines (e = Bvl for a rod moving perpendicular to B). It depends on: (i) the magnetic flux density B, (ii) the length l of the conductor, and (iii) the velocity v with which the conductor moves (and the angle between v and B).
keyPoints: Motional emf = Blv (rod moving ⊥ to B)
Depends on B, length l, velocity v

subject: Physics
text: (i) What is the ratio of the speed of gamma rays to that of radio waves in vacuum? (ii) Name an electromagnetic wave which is used in the radar system used in aircraft navigation.
modelAnswer: (i) Both gamma rays and radio waves are electromagnetic waves, so both travel at the speed of light c in vacuum. The ratio is 1:1. (ii) Microwaves are used in radar systems for aircraft navigation.
keyPoints: All EM waves travel at c in vacuum → ratio = 1

text: A biconvex lens made of glass (refractive index 1·5) has two spherical surfaces having radii 20 cm and 30 cm. Calculate its focal length.

subject: Physics
text: State any two differences between primary rainbow and secondary rainbow.
modelAnswer: (i) Primary rainbow is formed by one internal reflection and two refractions inside water droplets; secondary rainbow is formed by two internal reflections and two refractions. (ii) In the primary rainbow, red is on the outer edge and violet on the inner edge; in the secondary rainbow, the order is reversed (violet outer, red inner). (iii) The secondary rainbow is fainter and its angular radius (~51°) is larger than that of the primary (~42°).
keyPoints: Primary: 1 internal reflection; Secondary: 2 internal reflections
Colour order reversed in secondary rainbow
Secondary rainbow is fainter, larger angular radius

subject: Physics
text: (i) State de Broglie hypothesis. (ii) With reference to photoelectric effect, define threshold wavelength.
modelAnswer: (i) De Broglie hypothesis states that every moving particle of matter is associated with a wave, called the matter wave (or de Broglie wave), whose wavelength is λ = h/p = h/(mv). (ii) Threshold wavelength (λ0) is the maximum wavelength of incident light which can just cause photoelectric emission from a given metal surface (below which no emission occurs, no matter how intense the light).
keyPoints: Threshold wavelength: maximum λ for which photoemission just occurs

subject: Physics
text: Calculate the minimum wavelength of the spectral line present in the Balmer series of hydrogen.
modelAnswer: Minimum wavelength in Balmer series corresponds to transition from n=∞ to n=2 (series limit). 1/λ = R(1/2² − 1/∞²) = R/4 = 1·097×10⁷/4 = 2·7425×10⁶ m⁻¹. So λ = 1/2·7425×10⁶ = 3·65×10⁻⁷ m = 365 nm.

subject: Physics
text: What is meant by pair annihilation? Write a balanced equation for the same.
modelAnswer: Pair annihilation is the process in which a particle and its antiparticle (e.g. an electron and a positron) collide and are converted entirely into energy, usually in the form of two gamma-ray photons (to conserve momentum). Equation: e⁻ + e⁺ → γ + γ (each photon of energy 0·511 MeV).

subject: Physics
text: What is meant by the terms half-life of a radioactive substance and binding energy of a nucleus?
modelAnswer: Half-life (T½) is the time taken for half of the radioactive nuclei in a given sample to disintegrate (or the activity to fall to half its initial value). Binding energy of a nucleus is the energy required to completely separate a nucleus into its constituent protons and neutrons (equivalently, the energy released when the nucleus is formed from free nucleons), given by ΔE = Δm c², where Δm is the mass defect.
keyPoints: Half-life: time for half the nuclei to decay
Binding energy = energy to split nucleus into free nucleons = Δmc²

subject: Physics
text: In a communication system, what is meant by modulation? State any two types of modulation.
modelAnswer: Modulation is the process of superimposing a low-frequency message (information) signal onto a high-frequency carrier wave, so that some characteristic (amplitude, frequency, or phase) of the carrier is varied in accordance with the message signal, enabling efficient transmission over long distances. Two types: Amplitude Modulation (AM) and Frequency Modulation (FM) (also Phase Modulation).
keyPoints: Modulation: superimposing message signal on carrier wave

subject: Physics
text: Obtain an expression for intensity of electric field at a point in end on position, i.e. axial position of an electric dipole.
modelAnswer: Consider a dipole of charges −q at A and +q at B, separated by 2l, dipole moment p = q(2l). For point P on the axis at distance r from the centre O: E+ (due to +q, at distance r−l) = kq/(r−l)², directed away from +q (along axis). E− (due to −q, at distance r+l) = kq/(r+l)², directed towards −q, i.e. same direction as E+ on the axial line beyond the dipole. Net field E = E+ − E− = kq[1/(r−l)² − 1/(r+l)²] = kq[( (r+l)² − (r−l)² ) / (r²−l²)²] = kq[4rl/(r²−l²)²] = k(2p·r)/(r²−l²)², where k=1/4πε0. For r >> l: E ≈ 2kp/r³ = (1/4πε0)(2p/r³), directed along the dipole axis (from −q to +q direction).
keyPoints: Direction: along dipole axis, from −q to +q

subject: Physics
text: Deduce an expression for equivalent capacitance C when three capacitors C1, C2 and C3 are connected in parallel.
modelAnswer: When capacitors C1, C2, C3 are connected in parallel across a battery of potential V, each capacitor has the same potential difference V across it but different charges: Q1=C1V, Q2=C2V, Q3=C3V. Total charge Q = Q1+Q2+Q3 = (C1+C2+C3)V. If Ceq is the equivalent capacitance, Q = CeqV. So CeqV = (C1+C2+C3)V, giving Ceq = C1+C2+C3.
keyPoints: Parallel: same V across each capacitor

subject: Physics
text: ε1 and ε2 are two batteries having emf of 34V and 10V respectively and internal resistance of 1Ω and 2Ω respectively. They are connected in a network: branch AF carries ε1 (34V,1Ω) with current I1 (F to A), branch CD carries ε2 (10V,2Ω) with current I2 (D to C), branch AB has 4Ω, branch BC has 4Ω, branch BE has 5Ω (carrying I1+I2), branch FE has 7Ω, branch ED has 7Ω. Using Kirchhoff's Laws of electrical networks, calculate the currents I1 and I2.
modelAnswer: Applying KVL to loop A-F-E-B-A: 34 − I1(1+4+7) − 5(I1+I2) = 0 → 34 − 17I1 − 5I2 = 0 ... (1). Applying KVL to loop D-C-B-E-D: 10 − I2(2+4+7) − 5(I1+I2) = 0 → 10 − 5I1 − 18I2 = 0 ... (2). Solving (1) and (2): from (1) 17I1+5I2=34; from (2) 5I1+18I2=10. Multiplying (1) by 18 and (2) by 5 and subtracting: 306I1 − 25I1 = 612 − 50 → 281I1=562 → I1 = 2A. Substituting in (1): 34+5I2=34 → I2 = 0A.

subject: Physics
text: An electric bulb is marked 200V, 100W. Calculate electrical resistance of its filament. If five such bulbs are connected in series to a 200V supply, how much current will flow through them?
modelAnswer: Resistance R = V²/P = 200²/100 = 400 Ω. When 5 such bulbs (each 400Ω) are connected in series, total resistance = 5×400 = 2000 Ω. Current I = V/Rtotal = 200/2000 = 0·1 A.

subject: Physics
text: For any prism, prove that: n or μ = sin[(A+δm)/2] / sin(A/2), where the terms have their usual meaning.
modelAnswer: At minimum deviation, the ray passes symmetrically through the prism, so angle of incidence i = angle of emergence e, and the two angles of refraction at the two surfaces are equal: r1 = r2 = r. Using A = r1+r2 = 2r, so r = A/2. Also, deviation δ = (i+e) − A; at minimum deviation δ=δm and i=e, so δm = 2i − A, giving i = (A+δm)/2. By Snell's law at the first surface: n = sin i / sin r = sin[(A+δm)/2] / sin(A/2).

subject: Physics
text: When two thin lenses are kept in contact, prove that their combined or effective focal length F is given by: 1/F = 1/f1 + 1/f2, where the terms have their usual meaning.
modelAnswer: For an object O placed on the axis, the first lens (focal length f1) forms an image I1 of the object; this acts as a virtual object for the second lens (focal length f2), which forms the final image I at distance v. For lens 1: 1/v1 − 1/u = 1/f1. For lens 2 (object distance = v1, since lenses are in contact): 1/v − 1/v1 = 1/f2. Adding: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f1 + 1/f2. But for the equivalent single lens producing the same image: 1/v − 1/u = 1/F. Hence 1/F = 1/f1 + 1/f2.
keyPoints: Apply lens formula successively to both lenses

subject: Physics
text: (i) In Young's double slit experiment, show graphically how intensity of light varies with distance. (ii) In Fraunhofer diffraction, how is the angular width of the central bright fringe affected when slit separation is increased?
modelAnswer: (i) In YDSE, the intensity varies as I = 4I0 cos²(φ/2), where φ is the phase difference between the two waves reaching a point. Plotted against position (or path difference), this gives a series of bright fringes (maxima, I=4I0) alternating with dark fringes (minima, I=0), i.e. a cosine-squared pattern of equal fringe width (all bright fringes are equally intense in ideal two-slit interference). (ii) In single-slit Fraunhofer diffraction, the angular width of the central maximum is 2λ/a, where a is the slit width. Note: 'slit separation' here refers to slit width a; as the slit width a is increased, angular width 2λ/a decreases, i.e. the central maximum becomes narrower.
keyPoints: Increasing slit width a → narrower central maximum

subject: Physics
text: Write one balanced equation each to show: (i) Nuclear fission (ii) Nuclear fusion (iii) Emission of β⁻ (i.e. a negative beta particle).
modelAnswer: (i) Nuclear fission: ₀n¹ + ₉₂U²³⁵ → ₅₆Ba¹⁴¹ + ₃₆Kr⁹² + 3₀n¹ + energy. (ii) Nuclear fusion: ₁H² + ₁H² → ₂He³ + ₀n¹ + energy (or ₁H² + ₁H³ → ₂He⁴ + ₀n¹ + energy). (iii) β⁻ emission: a neutron converts to a proton, electron and antineutrino: ZXᴬ → (Z+1)Yᴬ + ₋₁e⁰ + ν̄. E.g. ₉₀Th²³⁴ → ₉₁Pa²³⁴ + ₋₁e⁰ + ν̄.
keyPoints: Fission: heavy nucleus splits (e.g. U-235 + n → Ba+Kr+3n)
Fusion: light nuclei combine (e.g. deuterium+deuterium → He-3+n)

subject: Physics
text: With reference to semiconductor devices, define a p-type semiconductor and a Zener diode. What is the use of a Zener diode?
modelAnswer: A p-type semiconductor is formed by doping a pure (intrinsic) semiconductor such as silicon or germanium with a trivalent impurity (e.g. Boron, Indium), creating an excess of holes (majority carriers are holes). A Zener diode is a specially designed, heavily doped p-n junction diode meant to be operated in the reverse breakdown region, where it maintains a nearly constant voltage (Zener voltage) across it over a range of currents. Use: it is used as a voltage regulator, to provide a constant reference/output voltage in power supply circuits.
keyPoints: p-type: doped with trivalent impurity, holes are majority carriers
Zener diode: operates in reverse breakdown with constant voltage

subject: Physics
text: Draw a labelled ray diagram of an image formed by a refracting telescope with final image formed at infinity. Derive an expression for its magnifying power with the final image at infinity.
modelAnswer: An astronomical (refracting) telescope consists of an objective lens (large focal length fo, large aperture) and an eyepiece (small focal length fe), coaxially arranged, separated by a distance fo+fe (normal adjustment). Parallel rays from a distant object are focused by the objective at its focal plane, forming a real, inverted, diminished image. This image lies at the focal point of the eyepiece too (for final image at infinity), so the eyepiece produces a final virtual image at infinity, magnified further. The objective forms image of height h at distance fo; the angle subtended at the objective by the object equals α ≈ h/fo (angle without telescope). Angle subtended by the final image at the eye ≈ β ≈ h/fe. Magnifying power M = β/α = fo/fe. Thus for normal adjustment, M = fo/fe (with negative sign showing image is inverted), and the length of the telescope L = fo+fe.
keyPoints: Objective (large fo) forms real image at its focal plane
Eyepiece (small fe) magnifies this image, final image at infinity when object image at fe

subject: Physics
text: (i) Using Huygen's wave theory, derive Snell's law of refraction. (ii) With the help of an experiment, state how will you identify whether a given beam of light is polarised or unpolarised.
modelAnswer: (i) Consider a plane wavefront AB incident on a plane surface XY separating two media (refractive indices n1, n2), travelling with speeds v1 in medium 1 and v2 in medium 2. Let the wavefront take time t to travel from B to C (in medium 1) while the secondary wavelet from A travels to D (in medium 2): BC = v1t, AD = v2t. In triangle ABC, sin i = BC/AC = v1t/AC. In triangle ADC, sin r = AD/AC = v2t/AC. So sin i/sin r = v1/v2 = constant = n21 (refractive index of medium 2 w.r.t. medium 1), which is Snell's law. (ii) Pass the beam through a polaroid (analyser) and rotate the polaroid about the direction of propagation while observing the transmitted intensity. If the intensity varies periodically between a maximum and (nearly) zero as the polaroid is rotated through 360°, the incident light is polarised. If the intensity remains unchanged (constant) throughout the rotation, the light is unpolarised.
keyPoints: Huygens construction: sin i/sin r = v1/v2 = n21 (Snell's law)
Test: rotate a polaroid (analyser) in the beam
Intensity varies (max to ~0) → polarised; constant intensity → unpolarised

subject: Physics
text: (i) With reference to the forward characteristic curve of a junction diode, calculate the resistance of the diode. (ii) Draw separate energy band diagrams for conductors, semi-conductors and insulators and describe how they differ.
modelAnswer: (i) Forward (dynamic) resistance of the diode is found from the slope of the V-I curve: rf = ΔV/ΔI, calculated between two points on the forward characteristic (e.g. between V=0·4V and V=0·6V, corresponding current values read off the graph). (ii) Energy band description: In a conductor, the valence band and conduction band overlap (no forbidden gap), so electrons move freely — high conductivity. In a semiconductor, there is a small forbidden energy gap (~1 eV, e.g. 1·1eV for Si, 0·7eV for Ge) between valence and conduction bands, so some electrons can cross it at room temperature. In an insulator, the forbidden gap is very large (~>5 eV), so practically no electrons can jump to the conduction band, resulting in negligible conductivity.
keyPoints: Forward resistance rf = ΔV/ΔI from the graph slope

subject: Physics
text: A closed surface in vacuum encloses charges −q and +3q. The total electric flux emerging out of the surface is: (a) Zero (b) 2q/ε0 (c) 3q/ε0 (d) 4q/ε0
modelAnswer: (b) 2q/ε0. By Gauss's theorem, total flux = (net enclosed charge)/ε0 = (−q+3q)/ε0 = 2q/ε0.

subject: Physics
text: What is the angle of dip at a place where the horizontal component (BH) and vertical component (BV) of earth's magnetic field are equal: (a) 130° (b) 60° (c) 45° (d) 90°
modelAnswer: (c) 45°. tanδ = BV/BH = 1 (since BH=BV) → δ = 45°.

subject: Physics
text: A beam of light is incident at the polarizing angle of 35° on a certain glass plate. The refractive index of the glass plate is: (a) sin35° (b) tan35° (c) tan55° (d) sin55°
modelAnswer: (b) tan35°. By Brewster's law, n = tan(polarising angle) = tan35°.

subject: Physics
text: In a gamma ray emission from nucleus: (a) only the number of protons change. (b) the number of protons and neutrons, both change. (c) there is no change in the number of protons and the number of neutrons. (d) only the number of neutrons change.
modelAnswer: (c) There is no change in the number of protons and the number of neutrons. Gamma emission involves the nucleus losing energy (going from an excited to a lower energy state) by emitting a high-energy photon, without any change in atomic number or mass number.
keyPoints: Gamma decay: nucleus de-excites, emits photon
No change in Z (protons) or N (neutrons)

subject: Physics
text: The energy associated with light of which of the following colours is minimum: (a) violet (b) red (c) green (d) yellow
modelAnswer: (b) red. Photon energy E=hc/λ is inversely proportional to wavelength. Red light has the longest wavelength among visible colours, hence minimum photon energy.
keyPoints: E = hc/λ, inversely proportional to wavelength
Red has longest λ among options → minimum energy

subject: Physics
text: Define equipotential surface.
modelAnswer: An equipotential surface is a surface at every point of which the electric potential is the same; no work is done in moving a charge from one point to another on such a surface, and the electric field is always perpendicular to an equipotential surface.
keyPoints: No work done moving charge along it

subject: Physics
text: Calculate the net emf across A and B, given two 4V cells in series (same polarity) forming one branch between A and B, and an 8V cell forming another parallel branch directly between A and B.
modelAnswer: The top branch has two 4V cells in series (same polarity), giving a branch emf of 4+4 = 8V. The bottom branch is a single 8V cell. Both branches connecting A and B thus have equal emf (8V) and (assuming negligible/matched internal resistance) are in parallel with each other, so the net (terminal) emf across A and B is 8V — the two branches simply reinforce each other without driving any circulating current between them.
keyPoints: Equal emf branches in parallel → net emf across AB = 8V

subject: Physics
text: Why are the pole pieces of a horseshoe magnet in a moving coil galvanometer made cylindrical in shape?
modelAnswer: The cylindrical (concave) pole pieces, together with a soft iron cylindrical core, produce a radial magnetic field, i.e. the field is always parallel to the plane of the coil at every position of rotation. This ensures the magnetic torque on the coil (BINA) is directly proportional to the current I for all deflections, giving a uniform, linear scale.
keyPoints: Field always parallel to plane of coil
Ensures torque ∝ I uniformly → linear scale

subject: Physics
text: What is the value of power factor for a pure resistor connected to an alternating current source?
modelAnswer: For a pure resistor, current and voltage are in phase (phase difference φ=0), so power factor = cosφ = cos0° = 1.
keyPoints: Pure resistor: V and I in phase, φ=0

subject: Physics
text: What should be the path difference between two waves reaching a point for obtaining constructive interference in Young's Double Slit experiment?
modelAnswer: The path difference should be an integral multiple of the wavelength: Δ = nλ, where n = 0, 1, 2, 3, ...

subject: Physics
text: Define critical angle for a given medium.
modelAnswer: Critical angle is the angle of incidence (in the denser medium) for which the angle of refraction in the rarer medium is 90°; for angles of incidence greater than the critical angle, total internal reflection occurs.
keyPoints: Angle of incidence (denser medium) for which angle of refraction = 90°
Beyond this angle → total internal reflection

subject: Physics
text: Name the series in the atomic spectra of the hydrogen atom that falls in the ultra violet region.
modelAnswer: The Lyman series falls in the ultraviolet region of the hydrogen spectrum (transitions to n=1 from higher energy levels).

subject: Physics
text: In a potentiometer experiment, the balancing length with a resistance of 2Ω is found to be 100 cm, while that of an unknown resistance is 500 cm. Calculate the value of the unknown resistance.
modelAnswer: Since balancing length is proportional to the resistance (for the same current in a resistance-comparison potentiometer experiment), R1/l1 = R2/l2 → R2 = R1×l2/l1 = 2×500/100 = 10Ω.

subject: Physics
text: A rectangular loop of area 5m², has 50 turns and carries a current of 1 A. It is held in a uniform magnetic field of 0·1T, at an angle of 30°. Calculate the torque experienced by the coil.
modelAnswer: Torque τ = NIAB sinθ = 50×1×5×0·1×sin30° = 25×0·5 = 12·5 N·m. (Here θ is the angle between the plane of the coil and the field, or equivalently between the normal and B depending on convention; taking θ=30° as given, τ = NBIA sinθ = 12·5 N·m.)

subject: Physics
text: An electric current I flows through an infinitely long straight conductor. Write an expression and direction for the magnetic field at a point P at perpendicular distance r from the wire.
modelAnswer: Magnetic field at P: B = μ0I/(2πr). Direction: given by the right-hand thumb rule — if the thumb points in the direction of current flow, the curled fingers give the direction of the magnetic field, which forms concentric circles around the wire, perpendicular to the plane containing the wire and P.

subject: Physics
text: Three capacitors of capacitance C1=3µF, C2=6µF and C3=10µF are connected to a 10V battery: C1 and C2 are in series with each other, and this series combination is connected in parallel with C3, the whole combination across the 10V battery. subject: Physics
text: Obtain the balancing condition for the Wheatstone bridge arrangement, with arms P, Q, R, S, a galvanometer G between the P-Q and R-S junctions, and a battery E driving current I which splits into I1 (through P, R) and I2 (through Q, S).
modelAnswer: At balance, no current flows through the galvanometer, so the same current I1 flows through P and R, and I2 through Q and S. Since no current flows through G, the potential at the junction of P,Q equals the potential at the junction of R,S. This gives: I1P = I2Q (equal potential drop across P and Q) and I1R = I2S (equal potential drop across R and S). Dividing: P/Q = R/S, which is the balancing condition of the Wheatstone bridge.

subject: Physics
text: Derive the law of reflection using Huygen's Wave Theory.
modelAnswer: Let a plane wavefront AB be incident on a reflecting surface MN at angle of incidence i. While the secondary wavelet from B travels to C on the surface (in time t, BC=vt), the secondary wavelet from A (which reaches the surface earlier) reflects and travels an equal distance AD=vt in the same time (since both travel in the same medium with the same speed v). In right triangles ABC and ADC (common hypotenuse AC): sin i = BC/AC = vt/AC, and sin r (angle of reflection) = AD/AC = vt/AC. Since BC=AD=vt, sin i = sin r, so i = r. Also the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane. This proves the laws of reflection.
keyPoints: BC = AD = vt (equal in same medium)
sin i = sin r → i = r (law of reflection)

subject: Physics
text: State any two Bohr's postulates and write the energy value of the ground state of the hydrogen atom.
modelAnswer: Bohr's postulates: (i) Electrons revolve around the nucleus only in certain stable, non-radiating circular orbits, called stationary states, for which the angular momentum is quantised: mvr = nh/2π (n=1,2,3,...). (ii) An atom radiates energy only when an electron jumps from a higher energy orbit to a lower energy orbit, the energy of the emitted photon being equal to the difference in energies of the two orbits: hν = E2 − E1. The energy of the ground state (n=1) of the hydrogen atom is E1 = −13·6 eV.
keyPoints: Postulate 1: quantised angular momentum mvr = nh/2π
Postulate 2: photon emitted/absorbed on transition, hν=E2−E1

subject: Physics
text: With reference to semi-conductors answer the following: (i) What is the change in the resistance of the semi-conductor with increase in temperature? (ii) Name the majority charge carriers in n-type semi-conductor. (iii) What is meant by doping?
modelAnswer: (i) The resistance of a semiconductor decreases with increase in temperature (it has a negative temperature coefficient of resistance), because more electron-hole pairs are generated, increasing conductivity. (ii) The majority charge carriers in an n-type semiconductor are free electrons. (iii) Doping is the process of deliberately adding a small, controlled amount of impurity atoms (pentavalent or trivalent) to a pure (intrinsic) semiconductor to increase its conductivity and control its type (n-type or p-type).

Doping: adding controlled impurity to intrinsic semiconductor

text: (i) An alternating emf of 200V, 50Hz is applied to an L-R circuit, having a resistance R of 10Ω and an inductance L of 0·05H connected in series. Calculate: (1) Impedance. subject: Physics
text: Draw a neat labelled ray diagram showing the formation of an image at the least distance of distinct vision D by a simple microscope. When the final image is at D, derive an expression for its magnifying power at D.
modelAnswer: A simple microscope is a single convex lens of short focal length f. The object is placed between the lens and its focus (u<f), so that a virtual, erect, magnified image is formed at the near point (distance D from the eye, u negative, v=−D). Using lens formula 1/v−1/u=1/f with v=−D: 1/(−D) − 1/u = 1/f → 1/u = −1/D − 1/f. Magnifying power M = v/u (angular magnification for simple microscope = D/|u|, and using the lens relation this simplifies to): M = 1 + D/f. This is the magnifying power when the final image is formed at the near point D.
keyPoints: Object between lens and F (u<f); image virtual, erect, magnified, at near point D

subject: Physics
text: Draw a neat labelled diagram of Young's Double Slit experiment. Show that fringe width β = λD/d, where the terms have their usual meaning (either for bright or dark fringe).
modelAnswer: Two narrow, coherent slits S1 and S2 (separated by distance d) are illuminated by a monochromatic source, and a screen is placed at distance D from the slits (D>>d). For a point P on the screen at distance x from the centre O, the path difference is Δ = S2P − S1P ≈ xd/D (using the geometry of the setup, D>>d, small angle approximation). For a bright fringe (constructive interference): Δ = nλ → xd/D = nλ → xn = nλD/d. For the (n+1)th bright fringe, x(n+1) = (n+1)λD/d. Fringe width β = x(n+1) − xn = λD/d. (Similarly for dark fringes, Δ=(n+½)λ, and consecutive dark fringes are also separated by the same β=λD/d.)
keyPoints: Path difference at P: Δ ≈ xd/D
Bright fringe: xd/D = nλ → xn = nλD/d

subject: Physics
text: (i) Draw a labelled circuit diagram of a half wave rectifier and give its output waveform. (ii) Draw a symbol for NOR gate and write its truth table.
modelAnswer: (i) A half-wave rectifier uses a single p-n junction diode connected in series with the secondary of a step-down transformer and a load resistor RL. During the positive half-cycle of the AC input, the diode is forward biased and conducts, so current flows through RL, producing a pulse of output voltage. During the negative half-cycle, the diode is reverse biased and does not conduct, so output voltage is zero. Thus the output waveform consists of only the positive half-cycles of the input, repeated every full cycle (unidirectional, pulsating DC), i.e. only half of each input cycle is 'rectified' and passed to the output. (ii) NOR gate = OR gate followed by NOT (inverted OR). Truth table: A=0,B=0→Y=1; A=0,B=1→Y=0; A=1,B=0→Y=0; A=1,B=1→Y=0. (Y=1 only when both inputs are 0.)

NOR truth table: Y=1 only when A=0,B=0

subject: Physics
text: Show that intensity of electric field E at a point in broadside on position is given by: E = (1/4πε0) × p/(r²+l²)^(3/2), where the terms have their usual meaning.
modelAnswer: Consider a dipole with −q at A and +q at B, separated by 2l, centre O. For a point P on the perpendicular bisector (broadside/equatorial line) at distance r from O, distance of P from each charge = √(r²+l²). E+ (due to +q) and E− (due to −q) both have magnitude kq/(r²+l²), directed along AP and PB respectively. Their components perpendicular to the axis cancel (by symmetry), while components parallel to the axis (anti-parallel to dipole moment direction) add up. Each field makes an angle θ with the axis where cosθ = l/√(r²+l²). Net field E = 2×[kq/(r²+l²)]×cosθ = 2kq/(r²+l²) × l/√(r²+l²) = 2kql/(r²+l²)^(3/2) = kp/(r²+l²)^(3/2) = (1/4πε0)×p/(r²+l²)^(3/2), directed opposite to the dipole moment (parallel to axis, from +q side to −q side).
keyPoints: P on perpendicular bisector, distance from each charge = √(r²+l²)

subject: Physics
text: A parallel plate capacitor is charged by a battery, which is then disconnected. A dielectric slab having dielectric constant K, is now introduced between its two plates in order to occupy the space completely. modelAnswer: Since the battery is disconnected, the charge Q on the plates remains constant. (i) Capacitance increases: C' = KC (K times the original capacitance). (ii) Potential difference decreases: since Q is constant and C increases, V' = Q/C' = Q/(KC) = V/K (decreases to 1/K times original). (iii) Energy stored decreases: U' = Q²/(2C') = Q²/(2KC) = U/K (decreases to 1/K times original).

subject: Physics
text: E1 and E2 are two batteries having emfs of 3V and 4V and internal resistances of 2Ω and 1Ω respectively. E1 (with series resistor R1=4Ω) and E2 (with series resistor R2=7Ω) are connected between a common top node and a common bottom node, with a resistor R3=8Ω also connected directly between the same top and bottom nodes. Using Kirchhoff's Laws, calculate the currents I1 and I2 (through the E1 and E2 branches respectively).
modelAnswer: Let V be the potential of the top common node relative to the bottom node (0V). Branch 1 (E1, total resistance 2+4=6Ω): current entering top node I1 = (E1−V)/6 = (3−V)/6. Branch 2 (E2, total resistance 1+7=8Ω): current entering top node I2 = (E2−V)/8 = (4−V)/8. Branch 3 (R3=8Ω only): current leaving top node = V/8. By KCL: I1+I2 = V/8. So (3−V)/6 + (4−V)/8 = V/8. Multiplying throughout by 24: 4(3−V)+3(4−V) = 3V → 12−4V+12−3V = 3V → 24 = 10V → V = 2·4V. I1 = (3−2·4)/6 = 0·6/6 = 0·1A. I2 = (4−2·4)/8 = 1·6/8 = 0·2A.
keyPoints: Millman's theorem / KCL at common top node

subject: Physics
text: For two thin lenses kept in contact with each other, show that: 1/F = 1/f1 + 1/f2, where the terms have their usual meaning.
modelAnswer: For an object O on the axis, the first lens (f1) forms an intermediate image at v1, related by 1/v1 − 1/u = 1/f1. This image acts as the object for the second lens (f2), placed at the same location (lenses in contact), giving 1/v − 1/v1 = 1/f2, where v is the final image distance. Adding the two equations: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f1 + 1/f2. For the equivalent single lens of focal length F producing the same final image directly from the object: 1/v − 1/u = 1/F. Comparing: 1/F = 1/f1 + 1/f2.
keyPoints: Apply lens formula for each lens in succession

subject: Physics
text: A compound microscope consists of two convex lenses having focal length of 1·5cm and 5cm. When an object is kept at a distance of 1·6cm from the objective, the final image is virtual and lies at a distance of 25cm from the eyepiece. Calculate magnifying power of the compound microscope in this set-up.
modelAnswer: For the objective (f0=1·5cm, u0=−1·6cm): 1/v0 − 1/u0 = 1/f0 → 1/v0 = 1/f0 + 1/u0 = 1/1·5 + 1/(−1·6) = 0·6667 − 0·625 = 0·0417 → v0 = 24 cm. Magnification by objective m0 = v0/u0 = 24/(−1·6) = −15. For the eyepiece (fe=5cm), image at near point ve=−25cm (virtual image at D=25cm): magnification by eyepiece me = 1 + D/fe = 1+25/5 = 6. Total magnifying power M = m0×me = (−15)×6 = −90 (magnitude 90).
